"'''Maniac'''" is a song by American musician [[Michael Sembello]], co-written with Dennis Matkosky, and best known for its inclusion on the [[Flashdance (soundtrack)|soundtrack]] of the 1983 film ''[[Flashdance]]''. Originally conceived as a darkly humorous track inspired by a television report concerning a serial killer, and the 1980 horror film ''[[Maniac (1980 film)|Maniac]]'', the song was later rewritten with new lyrics at the request of ''Flashdance'' director [[Adrian Lyne]] and music supervisor [[Phil Ramone]] to better align with the film's narrative about a young dancer's intense training and ambition. The revised version was featured prominently in a key sequence of the film, accompanying a montage of the protagonist's home workout routine.

Following the unexpected commercial success of ''Flashdance'', [[Paramount Pictures]] produced a music video for "Maniac" using scenes from the film, which premiered on [[MTV]] in May 1983. The video's heavy rotation helped propel the single to number one on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], where it remained for two weeks, and contributed to the film's broader cultural impact. The success of "Maniac" played a significant role in establishing the music video as a viable and powerful tool for promoting motion pictures. The song earned multiple [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] nominations and was included on Sembello's debut album, ''[[Bossa Nova Hotel]]'', though he distanced himself from attempts to replicate its style. "Maniac" later inspired cover versions and remixes, including a [[Maniac 2000|2000 Irish hit]] that became one of the country's best-selling singles of all time.

"Maniac" is a song by American musician Michael Sembello, co-written with Dennis Matkosky, and best known for its inclusion on the soundtrack of the 1983 film Flashdance. Originally conceived as a darkly humorous track inspired by a television report concerning a serial killer, and the 1980 horror film Maniac, the song was later rewritten with new lyrics at the request of Flashdance director Adrian Lyne and music supervisor Phil Ramone to better align with the film's narrative about a young dancer's intense training and ambition. The revised version was featured prominently in a key sequence of the film, accompanying a montage of the protagonist's home workout routine.

Following the unexpected commercial success of Flashdance, Paramount Pictures produced a music video for "Maniac" using scenes from the film, which premiered on MTV in May 1983. The video's heavy rotation helped propel the single to number one on the Billboard Hot 100, where it remained for two weeks, and contributed to the film's broader cultural impact. The success of "Maniac" played a significant role in establishing the music video as a viable and powerful tool for promoting motion pictures. The song earned multiple Grammy nominations and was included on Sembello's debut album, Bossa Nova Hotel, though he distanced himself from attempts to replicate its style. "Maniac" later inspired cover versions and remixes, including a 2000 Irish hit that became one of the country's best-selling singles of all time.

sections.heading: Composition and recording
sections.wikitext:
[[File:Phil ramone.jpg|thumb|Phil Ramone produced the song with Sembello.|left]]The general concept for what became the ''Flashdance'' hit came to songwriter Dennis Matkosky while watching a news report about a [[serial killer]].<ref>{{cite video|people= Matkosky, Dennis |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= I was watching the news one night, and—we were living in the valley—and they found all these bodies.}}</ref> He jokingly thought, "With my luck, this guy lives next door to me," and immediately jotted down the lyrics that came to mind: "He's a maniac. He just moved in next door. He'll kill your cat and nail it to the floor."<ref>{{cite video|people= Matkosky, Dennis |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= So I just wrote down on a piece of paper while I'm watching—I'm just doodling, 'He's a maniac. He just moved in next door. He'll kill your cat and nail it to the floor.'}}</ref> He took the idea to his friend Michael Sembello, whose eyes widened with interest when he heard the title.<ref>{{cite video|people= Matkosky, Dennis |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= So I go over to Michael's house, and I say to Michael…, "What do you think of this title?" I say, "Maniac," and his eyes get real wide.}}</ref> As soon as Matkosky was seated at a piano, Sembello said, "All right. Hit the weirdest chord you know," and they began composing the music.<ref name="Dennis">{{cite video|people= Matkosky, Dennis |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]]}}</ref> Their inspiration for the [[Bridge (music)|bridge]] came from the [[Bloodrock]] song "[[D.O.A. (song)|D.O.A.]]",<ref>{{cite video|people= Matkosky, Dennis |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= And then when it came to the [[Bridge (music)|B-section]], there was a song that we had heard as kids called "[[D.O.A. (song)|D.O.A.]]"—dead on arrival—and it used the English ambulance, which was—musically terms—a [[tritone]]… So we put that in there, and that was the B-section.}}</ref> a number 36 hit on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] in 1971<ref>{{Harvnb|Whitburn|2009|p=104}}</ref> that recreated the two-tone siren used on ambulances in the United Kingdom at that time,<ref name="Dennis"/> and Sembello came up with the idea of using "[[Chopsticks (waltz)|Chopsticks]]" to introduce the instrumental portion of the song.<ref>{{cite video|people= Matkosky, Dennis |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= When it came to the solo section, Michael goes, 'What about a mongoloid playing "[[Chopsticks (waltz)|Chopsticks]]"'? So he went over to the piano and started playing [[Tone cluster|clusters]].}}</ref> Matkosky said, "We thought it was a joke because we weren't trying to write a song. We were trying to make our friends laugh."<ref name="Dennis"/>

Sembello recalled their usual process for situations where they needed more lyrics: "Whenever we get an idea, we start researching, but we didn't have Google."<ref>{{cite video|people= Sembello, Michael |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]]}}</ref> Matkosky found the 1980 slasher film ''[[Maniac (1980 film)|Maniac]]'' and rented it to see if they could come up with more to put in the song.<ref>{{cite video|people= Sembello, Michael |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= [Dennis] came over… we were sitting,… trying to come up with lyrics. And [Dennis] said, "Hey, I found a movie called ''[[Maniac (1980 film)|Maniac]]''. Let's look at"--and we watched the movie, and we're going—he brought the movie over.}}</ref> It did provide the additional lyrics they wanted,<ref>{{cite video|people= Sembello, Michael |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= and we're just, like, watching the movie, and thinking of, like, horror stuff.}}</ref> but the demo they recorded wound up on a tape sent to [[Phil Ramone]], who was looking for songs to use in ''Flashdance''.<ref>{{Harvnb|Bronson|2003|p=576}}: When his friend Phil Ramone called and asked if Michael had anything suitable for the upcoming ''Flashdance'' motion picture, Sembello sent a demo tape without realizing that "Maniac" was included.</ref> During the film's pre-production, the two-tone siren music used in the bridge stood out for the film's director, [[Adrian Lyne]], who said, "One of the tunes I'd heard had a kind of a chime in it, that kind of 'bing-bong-bing-bong-bing-bong', like that, and I said, 'Let's use that. Let's use that as a kind of a motive, as a kind of a driving thing for a dance.'"<ref>{{cite video|people= Lyne, Adrian |year= 2010 |title= Flashdance: Music and Songs (''bonus feature from'' Flashdance, Special Collector's Edition) |medium= DVD |publisher= Paramount}}</ref> Lyne had grown accustomed to using the music by the end of filming and wanted it in the final cut,<ref>{{cite video|people= Ramone, Phil |year= 2010 |title= Flashdance: Music and Songs (''bonus feature from'' Flashdance, Special Collector's Edition) |medium= DVD |publisher= Paramount |quote= At the end of it, Adrian Lyne, the director, had gotten used to it, and they said, 'OK, this is gonna stay in the picture.'}}</ref> so Ramone asked for lyrics to fit the movie<ref>{{cite video|people= Matkosky, Dennis |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= He says,… 'The only way you're ever gonna get this song cut is if you rewrite the lyrics to the script.'}}</ref> and had Sembello re-record the song.<ref>{{cite video|people= Ramone, Phil |year= 2010 |title= Flashdance: Music and Songs (''bonus feature from'' Flashdance, Special Collector's Edition) |medium= DVD |publisher= Paramount |quote= So he and I scrambled and finished what was a little demo made in a cottage-type studio.}}</ref>
sections.text:
thumb|Phil Ramone produced the song with Sembello.|leftThe general concept for what became the Flashdance hit came to songwriter Dennis Matkosky while watching a news report about a serial killer. He jokingly thought, "With my luck, this guy lives next door to me," and immediately jotted down the lyrics that came to mind: "He's a maniac. He just moved in next door. He'll kill your cat and nail it to the floor." He took the idea to his friend Michael Sembello, whose eyes widened with interest when he heard the title. As soon as Matkosky was seated at a piano, Sembello said, "All right. Hit the weirdest chord you know," and they began composing the music. Their inspiration for the bridge came from the Bloodrock song "D.O.A.", a number 36 hit on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1971 that recreated the two-tone siren used on ambulances in the United Kingdom at that time, and Sembello came up with the idea of using "Chopsticks" to introduce the instrumental portion of the song. Matkosky said, "We thought it was a joke because we weren't trying to write a song. We were trying to make our friends laugh."

Sembello recalled their usual process for situations where they needed more lyrics: "Whenever we get an idea, we start researching, but we didn't have Google." Matkosky found the 1980 slasher film Maniac and rented it to see if they could come up with more to put in the song. It did provide the additional lyrics they wanted, but the demo they recorded wound up on a tape sent to Phil Ramone, who was looking for songs to use in Flashdance. During the film's pre-production, the two-tone siren music used in the bridge stood out for the film's director, Adrian Lyne, who said, "One of the tunes I'd heard had a kind of a chime in it, that kind of 'bing-bong-bing-bong-bing-bong', like that, and I said, 'Let's use that. Let's use that as a kind of a motive, as a kind of a driving thing for a dance.'" Lyne had grown accustomed to using the music by the end of filming and wanted it in the final cut, so Ramone asked for lyrics to fit the movie and had Sembello re-record the song.

sections.heading: Music video
sections.wikitext: Before ''Flashdance'' was released on April 15, 1983,<ref name="Ressner">{{cite magazine|first= Jeffrey |last= Ressner |title= Polygram Gears Up Push for ''Flashdance'' LP |magazine= [[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]] |date= May 7, 1983 |volume= XLIV |issue= 49 |pages= 10, 18 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/80s/1983/Cash-Box-1983-05-07.pdf}}</ref> its distributor [[Paramount Pictures]] had doubts that it would do well at the box office.<ref>{{Harvnb|Eszterhas|2010|p=171}}: "Paramount had so little faith in ''Flashdance'' that the studio sold off 30 percent of its own potential profit to a private investors group. We all knew, of course, that studios only did that with movies that they were absolutely certain would stiff."</ref> The May 7 issue of ''Cash Box'', however, reported on the surprise success of the film and Paramount's plan to have Lyne take parts of scenes from it to create music videos to be shown on the cable channel [[MTV]] as well as on television programs and at other venues featuring such clips.<ref name="Ressner"/> "Maniac" was listed on the reports that MTV provided to ''Billboard'' that indicated what videos were in rotation on the cable network and made its first appearance there in the May 21 issue, which indicated that it had been added to their playlist as of May 11.<ref>{{cite magazine|title= Video Music Programming |magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |date= May 21, 1983 |volume= 95 |issue= 21 |page= 20 |issn= 0006-2510 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/80s/1983/BB-1983-05-21.pdf}}</ref>
sections.text: Before Flashdance was released on April 15, 1983, its distributor Paramount Pictures had doubts that it would do well at the box office. The May 7 issue of Cash Box, however, reported on the surprise success of the film and Paramount's plan to have Lyne take parts of scenes from it to create music videos to be shown on the cable channel MTV as well as on television programs and at other venues featuring such clips. "Maniac" was listed on the reports that MTV provided to Billboard that indicated what videos were in rotation on the cable network and made its first appearance there in the May 21 issue, which indicated that it had been added to their playlist as of May 11.

sections.heading: Release and commercial performance
sections.wikitext: The June 4, 1983, issue of ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]'' magazine included the first appearance of the [[Single (music)#7-inch format|7-inch single]] of "Maniac" on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]], where it spent 22 weeks,<ref name="Sembello">{{Harvnb|Whitburn|2009|p=869}}</ref> and the September 10 ''Billboard'' marked its first of 2 weeks as the most popular song in the US.<ref name="Bronson">{{cite book|first= Fred |last= Bronson |year= 1992 |title= The Billboard Book of Number One Hits |publisher= Billboard Publications |location= New York, NY |pages= [https://archive.org/details/billboardbookofn0000bron/page/576 576-577] |isbn= 0-8230-8298-9 |url= https://archive.org/details/billboardbookofn0000bron/page/576}}</ref> It reached number 34 during its 8 weeks on the magazine's Top Rock Tracks chart that began in the July 30 issue,<ref>{{Harvnb|Whitburn|2008|p=224}}</ref> and also made a number 34 showing over the course of 9 weeks on the [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Adult Contemporary]] chart as of the September 3 ''Billboard''.<ref name="SembelloAC">{{Harvnb|Whitburn|2007|p=246}}</ref> Their September 10 Chartbeat column bemoaned the latter appearance as a "sign of the times", noting that "AC clearly isn't just for [[Anne Murray]] anymore",<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Paul |last= Grein |title= Chartbeat > ''Flashdance'': A Second Number One |magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |date= September 10, 1983 |volume= 95 |issue= 37 |page= 6 |issn= 0006-2510 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/80s/1983/BB-1983-09-10.pdf}}</ref> an uncannily prescient assessment considering that the song went to number 1 on the Adult Contemporary<ref name="AcCAN"/> and pop<ref name="CAN"/> charts in Murray's native [[Canada]] just weeks later. It also made the top 10 on the pop charts in Australia,<ref name="AUS"/> Germany,<ref name="GER"/> the Netherlands,<ref name="NL"/> New Zealand,<ref name="NZ"/> Spain,<ref name="SP"/> and Switzerland.<ref name="SWI"/> The [[Twelve-inch single|12-inch remix]] began 15 weeks on the Dance/Disco Top 80 in the June 25 ''Billboard'' and eventually got as high as number 6.<ref>{{Harvnb|Whitburn|2004|p=226}}</ref>
sections.text: The June 4, 1983, issue of Billboard magazine included the first appearance of the 7-inch single of "Maniac" on the Billboard Hot 100, where it spent 22 weeks, and the September 10 Billboard marked its first of 2 weeks as the most popular song in the US. It reached number 34 during its 8 weeks on the magazine's Top Rock Tracks chart that began in the July 30 issue, and also made a number 34 showing over the course of 9 weeks on the Adult Contemporary chart as of the September 3 Billboard. Their September 10 Chartbeat column bemoaned the latter appearance as a "sign of the times", noting that "AC clearly isn't just for Anne Murray anymore", an uncannily prescient assessment considering that the song went to number 1 on the Adult Contemporary and pop charts in Murray's native Canada just weeks later. It also made the top 10 on the pop charts in Australia, Germany, the Netherlands, New Zealand, Spain, and Switzerland. The 12-inch remix began 15 weeks on the Dance/Disco Top 80 in the June 25 Billboard and eventually got as high as number 6.

"Maniac" was selected as the best song on the soundtrack album by the editors of ''[[CD Review|Digital Audio]]{{'}}s Guide to Compact Discs'', who described how "it opens with a fast disco drum machine beat, augmented by frantic synthesizers and a pulsating bass line."<ref>{{Harvnb|Canale|1986|p=148}}</ref> In their retrospective reviews, [[AllMusic]] labeled the song as one of their Album Picks from the ''Flashdance'' soundtrack<ref>{{cite web|first= William |last= Ruhlmann |title= Original Soundtrack – Flashdance |publisher= [[Allmusic]] |accessdate= May 23, 2021 |url= https://www.allmusic.com/album/flashdance-original-soundtrack-mw0000193797}}</ref> and the 1994 ''[[Casablanca Records]] Story'' compilation.<ref>{{cite web|first= Stephen Thomas |last= Erlewine |author-link= Stephen Thomas Erlewine |title= Various Artists – Casablanca Records Story |publisher= [[Allmusic]] |accessdate= May 23, 2021 |url= https://www.allmusic.com/album/casablanca-records-story-mw0000119055}}</ref>

In their retrospective reviews, AllMusic labeled the song as one of their Album Picks from the Flashdance soundtrack and the 1994 Casablanca Records Story compilation.

sections.heading: Awards and accolades
sections.wikitext: As a single, "Maniac" earned Sembello [[Grammy Awards|Grammy]] nominations for [[Grammy Award for Record of the Year|Record of the Year]]<ref name="grammy361">{{Harvnb|O'Neil|1999|p=361}}</ref> and [[Grammy Award for Best Male Pop Vocal Performance|Best Pop Vocal Performance, Male]],<ref name="grammy362">{{Harvnb|O'Neil|1999|p=362}}</ref> and a nomination with Matkosky for [[Grammy Award for Song of the Year|Song of the Year]].<ref name="grammy362"/> As part of the [[Flashdance (soundtrack)|''Flashdance'' soundtrack]], it gave them and all of the songwriters who contributed to the album the [[Grammy Award for Best Score Soundtrack for Visual Media|Grammy Award for Best Album of Original Score Written for a Motion Picture or a Television Special]],<ref>{{Harvnb|O'Neil|1999|pp=367–368}}</ref> and Sembello was also nominated alongside all of the other performers on the soundtrack for [[Grammy Award for Album of the Year|Album of the Year]].<ref name = grammy361/> "Maniac" was nominated for the [[Academy Award for Best Original Song|Academy Award]]<ref>{{Harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=1143}}</ref> and [[Golden Globe Award for Best Original Song|Golden Globe]]<ref>{{Harvnb|O'Neil|2003|p=474}}</ref> for Best Original Song, and the music video for "Maniac" was awarded Best Editing at ''Billboard'' magazine's Video Music Awards.<ref>{{cite magazine|title= Jackson Cops Five Music Vid Awards |magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |date= November 26, 1983 |volume= 95 |issue= 48 |page= 60 |issn= 0006-2510 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/80s/1983/BB-1983-11-26.pdf}}</ref>
sections.text: As a single, "Maniac" earned Sembello Grammy nominations for Record of the Year and Best Pop Vocal Performance, Male, and a nomination with Matkosky for Song of the Year. As part of the Flashdance soundtrack, it gave them and all of the songwriters who contributed to the album the Grammy Award for Best Album of Original Score Written for a Motion Picture or a Television Special, and Sembello was also nominated alongside all of the other performers on the soundtrack for Album of the Year. "Maniac" was nominated for the Academy Award and Golden Globe for Best Original Song, and the music video for "Maniac" was awarded Best Editing at Billboard magazine's Video Music Awards.

sections.heading: Live performances
sections.wikitext: Some of Sembello's appearances to promote "Maniac" included programs where performers would [[lip sync]] to the hit recording of their song, such as ''[[Solid Gold (TV series)|Solid Gold]]'', where he appeared on June 18,<ref>{{cite episode|title= Marilyn McCoo & Rex Smith Show 37 |series= Solid Gold |series-link= Solid Gold (TV series) |air-date= June 18, 1983 |season= 3 |number= 37}}</ref> and ''[[American Bandstand]]'', which included a brief interview of him by [[Dick Clark]], on September 10.<ref>{{cite episode|title= Episode #27.1 |series= American Bandstand |series-link= American Bandstand |air-date= September 10, 1983 |season= 27 |number= 1}}</ref> At the [[56th Academy Awards]] on April 9, 1984, the song was performed live by [[Lani Hall]] with [[Herb Alpert]] & the Tijuana Brass.<ref>{{Harvnb|Wiley|Bona|1996|p=638}}</ref>
sections.text: Some of Sembello's appearances to promote "Maniac" included programs where performers would lip sync to the hit recording of their song, such as Solid Gold, where he appeared on June 18, and American Bandstand, which included a brief interview of him by Dick Clark, on September 10. At the 56th Academy Awards on April 9, 1984, the song was performed live by Lani Hall with Herb Alpert & the Tijuana Brass.

sections.heading: Legacy and influence
sections.wikitext:
{{Main|Flashdance (soundtrack)#Legacy and influence}}

The extensive exposure that the "Maniac" video received from MTV and other outlets helped Paramount plug ''Flashdance'' for free instead of paying the several million dollars of commercial time for the standard television advertising exposure needed to get the same result.<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Jack |last= Egan |title= Pop Records Go Boom |date= October 31, 1983 |magazine= [[New York (magazine)|New York]] |publisher= News Group Publications |page= 55 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=meICAAAAMBAJ&pg=PA55 |quote= A clip of scenes from the movie done to the hit single 'Maniac' has been broadcast extensively on MTV and other outlets, helping to promote the movie at no cost to Paramount, which made the film. To purchase the same amount of commercial time on television would probably have cost several million dollars.}}</ref> Paramount vice president Gordon Weaver described this approach as "invisible marketing".<ref name="Harmetz">{{cite news|first= Aljean |last= Harmetz |title= 'Invisible Marketing' Helps 'Flashdance' Sell |newspaper= [[The New York Times]] |location= New York |department= Section 1 |page= 15 |date= June 4, 1983 |url= https://www.nytimes.com/1983/06/04/movies/invisible-marketing-helps-flashdance-sell.html}}</ref> ''Flashdance'' went on to be the third highest-grossing film of 1983 in the US<ref>{{cite web|title= Domestic Box Office for 1983 |website= [[Box Office Mojo]] |publisher= [[IMDb]] |access-date= July 24, 2021 |url= https://boxofficemojo.com/yearly/chart/?yr=1983&p=.htm}}</ref> despite having unknown actors and receiving bad reviews, so the new priority for studio marketing departments became evaluating how practical it would be to include popular music in the projects they were looking to release in order to receive similar benefits from such outlets.<ref>{{cite news|first= Bob |last= McKelvey |title= Movies are catching dancing' fever and rakin' in big bucks |newspaper= [[Daily Press (Virginia)|The Daily Press]] |publisher= [[Tribune Publishing]] |location= [[Newport News, Virginia]] |date= June 2, 1984 |page= 17 |url= https://www.newspapers.com/clip/21324961/moviesarecatchingdancinfeverandrak/ |quote= As one Warners executive commented happily, 'Studios are evaluating the viability of music in every project.'}}</ref>
sections.text:
{{Main|Flashdance (soundtrack)#Legacy and influence}}

The extensive exposure that the "Maniac" video received from MTV and other outlets helped Paramount plug Flashdance for free instead of paying the several million dollars of commercial time for the standard television advertising exposure needed to get the same result. Paramount vice president Gordon Weaver described this approach as "invisible marketing". Flashdance went on to be the third highest-grossing film of 1983 in the US despite having unknown actors and receiving bad reviews, so the new priority for studio marketing departments became evaluating how practical it would be to include popular music in the projects they were looking to release in order to receive similar benefits from such outlets.

sections.heading: Aftermath
sections.wikitext:
In 1983, Sembello said, "It's a funny irony that it caught on so, especially since I don't dance and have never even been to a disco."<ref>{{cite magazine|first= Fred |last= Goodman |title= East Coastings |magazine= [[Cashbox (magazine)|Cash Box]] |date= November 19, 1983 |volume= XLV |issue= 25 |page= 11 |url= https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Cash-Box/80s/1983/CB-1983-11-19.PDF}}</ref> Later he expressed pride in having a number one record after working in the business for so many years, cautioning, "But, hey, let it die. 'Maniac' was just a song, and now I'm on to the next, and I don't want to rip off the record-buying public by doing a carbon-copy of 'Maniac' just to make some money."<ref name="Bronson"/> He chose to continue working with Ramone on his debut album, ''[[Bossa Nova Hotel]]'', which included his number one single and gave him two more U.S. chart hits: the number 34 Hot 100 entry "Automatic Man"<ref name="Sembello"/> and "Talk", which reached number 25 on the Adult Contemporary chart.<ref name="SembelloAC"/>

In May 2010, ''[[Maniac (1980 film)|Maniac]]'' director [[William Lustig]] interviewed Sembello and Matkosky to clear up the misconception that his film was what began the process of writing their song of the same name, and they confirmed that the story of how the song originated had been retold incorrectly over the years.<ref>{{cite video|people= Matkosky, Dennis |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= It's funny because I don't think anybody's ever gotten this story quite right.}}</ref><ref>{{cite video|people= Sembello, Michael |year= 2020 |title= Maniac Men (''bonus feature from'' Maniac: 4K Ultra HD + Special Features Blu-Ray) |medium= DVD |publisher= [[Blue Underground]] |quote= I've told [this story] in interviews and things, and it just never got [translated correctly].}}</ref>

In 1983, Sembello said, "It's a funny irony that it caught on so, especially since I don't dance and have never even been to a disco." Later he expressed pride in having a number one record after working in the business for so many years, cautioning, "But, hey, let it die. 'Maniac' was just a song, and now I'm on to the next, and I don't want to rip off the record-buying public by doing a carbon-copy of 'Maniac' just to make some money." He chose to continue working with Ramone on his debut album, Bossa Nova Hotel, which included his number one single and gave him two more U.S. chart hits: the number 34 Hot 100 entry "Automatic Man" and "Talk", which reached number 25 on the Adult Contemporary chart.

In May 2010, Maniac director William Lustig interviewed Sembello and Matkosky to clear up the misconception that his film was what began the process of writing their song of the same name, and they confirmed that the story of how the song originated had been retold incorrectly over the years.

sections.heading: Certifications
Other versions
sections.wikitext:
Irish [[rave music|rave]] act 4 Rhythm made a recording of "Maniac" in 1994 that replaced the verses with a more contemporary rap, but the publishers of the original, [[Warner Chappell Music]], "weren't happy with the change of lyrics and blocked the release".<ref name="hotpress">{{cite magazine|title= Triumph of the Underdog |magazine= [[Hot Press]] |date= March 12, 2001 |access-date= July 6, 2021 |url= https://www.hotpress.com/music/triumph-of-the-underdog-392085}}</ref> They did allow a 4 Rhythm version in which the original verses were rapped,<ref name="hotpress"/> and that recording reached number 28 in 1995, the same peak position that Sembello achieved, on the [[Irish Singles Chart]].<ref name="IRL"/> "[[Maniac 2000]]", a performance of [[Mark McCabe]] [[rapping]] over the 4 Rhythm version, spent ten weeks at number one on the Irish Singles Chart and became the country's fifth biggest-selling single of all time.<ref>{{cite web|title= "It was the total underdog": The real story behind Maniac 2000 |website= [[TheJournal.ie]] |date= March 4, 2015 |access-date= July 6, 2021 |url= https://www.thejournal.ie/maniac-2000-mark-mccabe-interview-1972681-Mar2015/}}</ref>

sections.text: Irish rave act 4 Rhythm made a recording of "Maniac" in 1994 that replaced the verses with a more contemporary rap, but the publishers of the original, Warner Chappell Music, "weren't happy with the change of lyrics and blocked the release". They did allow a 4 Rhythm version in which the original verses were rapped, and that recording reached number 28 in 1995, the same peak position that Sembello achieved, on the Irish Singles Chart. "Maniac 2000", a performance of Mark McCabe rapping over the 4 Rhythm version, spent ten weeks at number one on the Irish Singles Chart and became the country's fifth biggest-selling single of all time.
